title: Alone Against Fear - The Coming of the Dark Templars - The Tombs of the Blind Dead
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iHt3VLuizj4

Daniel (@dungeondive) opens with a film lesson: before Dawn of the Dead set off the Italian zombie boom, Spanish-Portuguese director Amando de Ossorio made the Blind Dead trilogy — slow, atmospheric, Hammer-influenced films about eyeless undead Templar knights in cloaks and armour, swinging two-handed claymores. Poorly paced and a little boring, he admits, but very metal.

Andrea Sfiligoi's The Coming of the Dark Templars brings that subgenre to Alone Against Fear as a standalone town crawl: visit farms, a funfair, a military installation and a mall, gather four clues and stop the knights' ritual. Two d6 tables generate Templars, the second nastier than the first, and there are new skills like medieval sword and lock picking. His new character Matthew Marvis — investigator, zombie hunter, tough and slippery, armed with a shotgun and a looted Templar sword — found all four clues and then died at the final showdown because he forgot to stop at the clinic first.

As a standalone, Daniel finds it lacking: few locations have their own charts, only two special events, not enough meat on the bone. Folded into the main campaign as a side quest, it shines. Travel rules link the two towns, and the spoiler: lose here and every future character is haunted by the Dark Templars, unique undead rolled from the Templar tables until you return and finish the job. He has gone further, canonising the black-robed knight that killed Marvis as a recurring slasher for his next campaign.

----

A lost side quest that haunts every future character — the Dark Templars become a curse on the whole campaign. What's the best cross-scenario consequence you've met in a solo game?
